simple.headline: TCP/IP is the real-world language of the internet
paragraphs: While OSI is a theoretical model with 7 layers, TCP/IP is what computers actually use — it has just 4 layers and powers everything from email to video calls.
IP addressing is like a home address — it tells routers where to deliver data. Every device on a network needs a unique IP address.
IPv4 uses 4 numbers (like 192.168.1.10) separated by dots. IPv6 uses 8 groups of hex numbers for a much larger address space.

technical.headline: RFC 1122 — The Internet Architecture
paragraphs: The TCP/IP model consolidates the OSI 7-layer model into 4 functional layers. It was developed by DARPA and is the foundation of the modern internet.
IPv4 addresses are 32-bit values written in dotted-decimal notation (four octets). Subnetting uses a subnet mask to divide an address into network and host portions.
CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) replaces classful addressing and uses prefix notation (e.g., /24) to indicate how many bits are the network portion.

layers.name: Application
layers.description: Combines OSI layers 5, 6, and 7. Handles all application-level protocols and data formatting.

layers.name: Transport
layers.description: End-to-end communication. TCP = reliable, connection-oriented. UDP = fast, connectionless.

layers.name: Internet
layers.description: Logical addressing and routing. Equivalent to OSI Layer 3. IP headers added here.

layers.name: Network Access
layers.description: Physical transmission and MAC addressing. Combines OSI Layers 1 and 2.

realWorld.headline: How your PC gets an IP address and sends data
realWorld.scenario: You plug your laptop into a network. Here's exactly what happens with IP addressing:
steps: Your NIC sends a DHCP Discover broadcast (255.255.255.255) to find a DHCP server
The DHCP server responds with an Offer: IP 192.168.1.50, mask 255.255.255.0, gateway 192.168.1.1
Your PC sends a DHCP Request to accept the offer
DHCP server sends ACK — your PC is now configured with IP, mask, gateway, and DNS
You ping 8.8.8.8: your PC checks if 8.8.8.8 is on your subnet — it's not (/24), so it sends to the default gateway
Your router (192.168.1.1) routes the packet out to the internet toward 8.8.8.8
ARP is used at each hop to resolve the next-hop router's MAC address for frame delivery

commonMistakes.headline: Exam traps on TCP/IP and IP addressing

mistakes.mistake: Confusing OSI and TCP/IP layer counts
mistakes.correction: OSI has 7 layers; TCP/IP has 4. The TCP/IP Application layer covers OSI layers 5, 6, and 7. The TCP/IP Network Access layer covers OSI layers 1 and 2.
mistakes.examTip: Questions about real-world protocols use TCP/IP (4 layers). Questions about layer concepts often refer to OSI (7 layers). Know both.

mistakes.correction: A /24 provides only 254 usable hosts (256 - 2 for network and broadcast). For 300 hosts you need /23 (510 usable) or /22 (1022 usable).
mistakes.examTip: Formula: usable hosts = 2^(host bits) - 2. Always subtract 2 for network and broadcast addresses.

mistakes.mistake: Thinking APIPA means the device has internet access
mistakes.correction: APIPA (169.254.x.x) means the device FAILED to get a DHCP address. The device assigned itself an address and can only communicate with other APIPA devices on the same segment.
mistakes.examTip: If a user says they have a 169.254.x.x address and cannot access the internet, check DHCP server availability.
